market_summary: The main event this week was the Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress in the US midterms. Traders took it as raising the odds of ending the Iran war, and Brent fell roughly 8-9% on Wednesday to a near two-month low. It was trading around $96-97 on Nov 5, well below the stale $107.03 Nov 3 mark. Hormuz risk has not gone away: the IRGC said two tankers and a tugboat caught fire on Nov 5 after allegedly using unauthorised routes. The Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on Oct 28, with two dissents in favour of a hike and markets pricing another hike. The US 10y is about 4.90% and the 2y about 4.59%. USD/JPY is near 158.4 with intervention worries, and the OAT-Bund spread is about 150bp after nearing 175bp on Oct 22 while the 2027 budget goes through the Assembly.

reasoning: Nothing clears the bar this week, and the account stays flat. (1) Oil: crude is pricing a binary outcome, a peace deal or continued attacks on Hormuz shipping. The Nov 3 marks are already $8-10 stale, so entry at the next official mark would come after a large, unknowable gap, and a stop tight enough to keep risk sensible would sit inside the daily noise. That leaves no edge in either direction (sources: tradingeconomics.com/commodity/crude-oil/news/598646; theglobeandmail.com/investing/article-oil-tumbles-as-investors-weigh-end-to-iran-war-after-us-democrats/; unitedagainstnucleariran.com/analysis/iran-shipping-update-november-5-2026). (2) US10Y: a lower oil price argues for a bond rally. Against that, the Fed has a hiking bias, with two dissents for a hike and a strong 55.5 ISM manufacturing reading. The 15bp fall in yields over the past week has already priced part of the oil move (sources: cnbc.com/2026/10/28/fed-interest-rate-decision-october-2026.html; seekingalpha.com/article/4958991). (3) JPY: there are arguments for a long. The US and Japan have intervened jointly before, and cheaper oil helps Japan's terms of trade. But MUFG notes persistent structural outflows and a weak link between rate gaps and the yen, and negative carry against a hiking Fed eats into any payoff. My honest probability is about 52%, which is not worth paying costs for (sources: tradingpedia.com/2026/11/04/yen-climbs-on-intervention-fears-softer-dollar/; tmgm.com MUFG yen note). (4) FR-DE: the spread could tighten further from 150bp or widen sharply again depending on the budget vote. I have no informational edge on that vote (source: pandaequityresearch.substack.com/p/the-spread-is-only-the-first-price). Finally, I used up my search budget before I could check the BoE decision, October payrolls, the BoJ and the ECB. Without those, I can't judge gilts, sterling, the euro, the Bund, the Swiss franc, the Aussie or the Canadian dollar. I will look again next week, once oil and the data have settled.

thesis: The 10y has fallen about 40bp in a month on lower oil and peace hopes, and a December hike is largely priced, so a benign October CPI could extend the rally into the 8-9 Dec FOMC. After The Opposition (December hike odds about 84%, not 94%; strong labour data) my view is about even, so size is the minimum needed to keep C06's two-position floor.

opposition.case_against: The thesis rests on a stale number. The 94% December-hike probability comes from the 14 October Citi/FedWatch note that followed the hot September CPI. Trading Economics puts December odds at about 84% on 10 November, up from about 74% a week earlier, and they fell as low as about 68-77% around the midterms. Hawkish repricing still has room to run, and the move is already in that direction. The labour data argue against a benign path: October payrolls were +165K against a 65K forecast, unemployment fell to 4.1%, jobless claims are at a 57-year low, productivity beat, and markets already price a further hike in 2027. The 10y depends on that terminal path, not only on the December decision. Inflation momentum is also adverse. September headline CPI was 3.7% (expected 3.6%) and core rose from 2.4% to 2.6% with a 0.3% m/m print, so price pressure is spreading beyond energy. The consensus for October already expects easing, which means a benign print is largely priced, while a core miss gets the trade stopped out. The oil leg is the weakest part. The 10y has already dropped about 40bp from 5.28% on peace hopes, yet in 2026 alone a June interim deal and a ceasefire collapsed, the August talks stalled over Iran's insistence on controlling and tolling Hormuz, and ships are still being attacked near the Strait. Finally, entry sits on the day CPI is released (10 November) with PPI on 13 November and the FOMC on 8-9 December. The stop is only 22-24bp away, well inside a normal one-month 1-sd 10y move of about 35-40bp at current vol, so the trade can be stopped out on noise even if the thesis turns out right.

thesis: Gilt yields are retreating from near-2007 highs as oil falls, and a 5%+ yield already discounts several further BoE hikes after the 5 Nov move to 4.0%. The Opposition's case (heavy fiscal supply, BoE hawkish guidance in December) leaves my view about even, so size is the minimum to meet C06's two-position floor.

opposition.case_against: The thesis is mostly priced in already. Brent has dropped from about $113 (29 Oct) to about $90 (9-10 Nov), and the 10y has rallied about 33bp in a month, to 5.11% on 10 Nov, its lowest since late August. Taking 'peace hopes' from here needs an actual deal, and this year an interim US-Iran deal already collapsed over the summer, while every round of talks has swung Brent by $5-10 on headlines. The BoE was explicit on 5 Nov that more tightening may be needed 'unless the war in Iran is resolved'. It projects CPI peaking at 4.9% in Q2 2027 (6.2% in the adverse case), with September core and services CPI above forecast. So October CPI (mid-November), labour data and Q3 GDP (Thursday, consensus a strong 0.7%) can all reprice the three further hikes the market expects by November 2027. Gilts are also following Treasuries: after a strong US jobs report, a December Fed hike is about 77-80% priced, which pulled gilt yields back above 5.15% on 6 Nov, so US CPI today and the FOMC are outside risks. The horizon also covers the December BoE meeting, where hawkish guidance would hit the trade directly. Fiscal headroom was cut from £24bn to £15bn in the 28 Oct budget, so supply and term premium are still a weak spot. Finally, the risk plan doesn't add up: the stop is at 5.40% but the stated change of mind is a close above 5.30%. The stop sits about 28bp away, roughly one month of recent realised movement (5.44 to 5.11 since late September), against a target that is never stated.
key_risks: Oil rebound: talks stall, Hormuz flows are disrupted again, or the Saudi-Iran front escalates. The summer interim deal already failed, and Brent moves $5-10 on single headlines.
Hot UK data: October CPI (with services or core still above forecast), wage data, or Q3 GDP at or above 0.7% would bring forward more BoE hikes.
December BoE meeting falls inside the horizon. Bailey's 'more tightening unless Iran is resolved' guidance is still in place, and the 8-1 vote shows no dovish group to restrain it.
US spillover: a December Fed hike is about 80% priced after strong payrolls, and a hot US CPI would lift global yields. Gilts already followed Treasuries higher on 6 Nov.
Fiscal and supply: headroom is down to £15bn, gilt issuance stays heavy, and the 6-month QT sales pause announced in September is temporary.
Mean reversion: a 33bp rally in a month into the bottom of a 5.1-5.44% range leaves little left to gain. Entering after the move gives poor reward for the risk.
Process: the stop (5.40%) and the change-of-mind level (5.30% close) disagree, and no target is set, so expected value can't be judged against the claimed 55%.

postmortem.assessment: The thesis needed a benign CPI and falling oil, and both went the other way within two sessions. The Opposition named exactly these risks (core at 0.3%, hike pricing with room to rise, repeated failures of US-Iran peace hopes, and a stop inside one month's normal range), and Janus's own probability after reading it was 50%, so the position expressed no view and existed only to meet C06's two-position floor. Taking a coin-flip long into a scheduled CPI release with a 17bp stop was a poor decision whatever the outcome; the size of the oil move on 12 November was bad luck, but the direction of the CPI risk was flagged in advance. The loss was contained because the size was the minimum.
postmortem.do_differently: 1. Do not open a position at a 50% probability to satisfy a count rule: C07 and then C08 already removed this, and the forecast record should lean to the side the evidence favours (here, The Opposition's side) rather than sit at even. 2. When The Opposition's case rests on a scheduled release inside the first days of the window, weight it more heavily in p_final. 3. Treat oil-driven rallies in long yields as fragile while Hormuz shipping is still being attacked.

postmortem.assessment: The direction was right over the one-day hold, but one day of a 20-trading-day question says nothing about skill, so the gain is luck. The decision that ended it was the weak part: a three-point move from 48 to 51, driven by the Opposition's carry and intervention arguments and a 'sharp overshoot' reading, flipped a position into the trend the day before the trend extended. Near 50, a flip turns a small conviction change into a full round trip of costs and a reversal of exposure.
postmortem.do_differently: 1) Do not cross 50 on an 'overshoot' argument alone when the fiscal driver is still worsening; require a concrete catalyst (intervention, a credible fiscal step) before flipping. 2) Treat moves of 1-3 points across 50 as costly: if the honest view is 'even', pick the side already held. 3) Check whether a local holiday (Brazil, 20 Nov) delays the base mark before reasoning about the overshoot being 'in the base mark'.

postmortem.assessment: A one-day holding cannot test a 20-trading-day thesis, so the result says nothing about the forecast; it will be judged when JF-series MXN forecasts resolve. The real decision to judge is the flip itself: moving from 51 to 49 on one day's news after the base mark had already absorbed it turned a near-even view into a round-trip cost for no information gain. With forecasts this close to 50, a one- or two-point change across 50 is noise, and C08 makes the book pay for it.
postmortem.do_differently: Treat a move across 50 by one or two points as needing new information that is not already in the base mark, not a re-reading of the same day's moves. When a forecast sits at 49-51, prefer keeping the previous side unless the evidence has clearly changed. Note that the 25% no-trade band does not protect against side flips, so near-even forecasts carry a cost each time they cross 50.

postmortem.assessment: A three-session hold says little about a 20-trading-day view, so the thesis is untested. But the haven risk that hurt it was already the live regime on 18 Nov (an equity drawdown under way), and the thesis anchored on a mid-November high and listed soft euro-area data, a yield-lowering factor, as support for higher yields. That is a process flaw, not only noise; the loss was small and partly costs from flipping a one-point lean.
postmortem.do_differently: 1) List the live market regime (equity drawdown, haven flows) among the drivers of every bond forecast, without assuming a fixed stock-bond sign while central banks are hiking. 2) Check that every cited driver points the same way as the forecast. 3) Avoid day-to-day side flips of one-point leans, which only generate costs.

opposition.case_against: Calling this 'luck' lets the process off the hook. The haven risk that sank the short was already the prevailing regime on 18 Nov, not a surprise. The S&P had fallen five sessions in a row and was 6.3% below its record, with the S&P down 3.1% on the week by that close. The VIX was in the 20s, and on 9 Nov the Bund had already hit its lowest since August on an earlier tech sell-off. The 'highest since late October' level near 3.4% was set on 13 Nov during an equity rebound that had already reversed by 18 Nov. So the thesis anchored on a stale high and left the live driver out. It also argued against itself: it cited 'euro-area data soft' as a reason for a yield-higher view it held at only 49%. On the lesson, an equity-haven rule is the wrong generalisation for this regime. With the Fed and ECB both hiking, stocks and bonds have not reliably moved in opposite directions: in the week of 6 Nov the S&P had its worst week since April 2025 while US 2y and 10y yields rose. The real lesson is that the position should not exist at 49%, or should be sized and banded so it cannot flip. The draft's '-8.6% S&P week' figure is not verified. Sources show about -5.1% Fri-to-Thu (7,561.67 to 7,175.83), and Friday's close could not be found. Trading Economics puts the Bund near or below 3.3% on 20 to 23 Nov, which does not match the book's marks of 3.39 and 3.37.
key_risks: Treating as noise a risk that was visible and in force at decision time (the AI equity drawdown and haven bid) understates a process error
The equity-haven lesson can mislead in a hiking regime where stocks and bonds have sometimes moved together (early-November data surprises)
The '-8.6% S&P week' figure in the draft is unverified and probably overstated (-5.1% Fri-to-Thu confirmed)
Book marks (3.39 / 3.37) may not match public closes near or below 3.3%, so the post-mortem P&L may be understated or use an inconsistent mark source
The thesis listed a yield-lowering factor (soft data) as support for a yield-higher call: an incoherence the draft does not mention
At 49% any outcome is 'luck' by construction, so the skill/luck field carries no information unless the forecaster's input set is audited

postmortem.assessment: Over three sessions of a 20-day question the outcome is mostly noise, and the overshoot-fade view at 51% was defensible: in the December 2024 precedent the central bank escalated after early sales failed and the real recovered within weeks. The judgement weakness was ignoring that one named catalyst (the fiscal-package vote and the first auction) had fired and failed before the fill, and that much of the overshoot had moved before the fill mark. Graded on the same standard as J027, it is mixed, not a clear skill failure.
postmortem.do_differently: 1) Before fading an EM sell-off, state what would anchor the currency (heavier intervention, a credible finance minister, a fiscal vote) and whether it is likely inside the window. 2) Account for the gap between the decision-day level and the next-day fill. 3) Do not flip one-point leans day to day; grade near-50 positions by one consistent standard.

opposition.case_against: The draft judges the same three-session hold by a different standard than J027. J027's 49% lean losing over three days is 'noise'. J033's 51% lean losing over three days is a 'judgement error'. A 1.4% move in USD/BRL at this volatility is under one 3-day sigma, and the 20-day window from 18 Nov runs to mid-December, so 'thesis_right: no' is premature. The asymmetry looks like outcome bias driven by a vivid narrative. The case for 'no' is real: the Senate finished voting on the fiscal package on 19 Nov, the market judged it insufficient, and the $1bn spot sale reversed the same day, so one named catalyst fired and failed. The lesson is still the wrong one. 'Treat a failed intervention as a momentum signal' and 'don't fade before an anchor' are the rules that would have been most wrong in the closest precedent, December 2024. Then the BCB's early interventions also failed, it kept going (about $27.8bn within days), and USD/BRL fell back from above 6.0 into the high-5s within roughly 20 to 30 trading days. By 19 Nov the dollar was up about 7.8% in November and more than 17% since the eve of the run-off. An overshoot fade at 51% was a defensible view, if tiny, not a skill failure. Two of the draft's drivers turned up in no search: 'uncertainty over the next finance minister' and 'foreign buying of dollar futures'. One cited fact is off: the dollar index was described as at its strongest since March 2025, while 16 Nov coverage says its highest close since April 2025.
key_risks: Grading two identical near-50 short holds by different standards (luck vs judgement error) adds outcome bias to the post-mortem record
'thesis_right: no' at day 3 of a 20-day horizon may flip by mid-December if the Chamber vote or heavier BCB action anchors the real, as in Dec 2024
The 'failed intervention = momentum' heuristic rests on one episode and is contradicted by the 2024 precedent, where intervention escalated
Drivers in the draft (finance-minister uncertainty, foreign futures buying) are unverified and may be invented narrative
The decision-to-fill gap (5.8102 to 5.8889, about 1.35%) is not discussed; part of the 'overshoot' had already been absorbed at fill, which bears on the entry rule rather than the view
Dollar-index date claim (March 2025) conflicts with reporting of the highest close since April 2025
